## Said Once

Somewhere between a third and a half of the distinct words in any book you pick up occur in it exactly once. Not once per chapter — once, total, in the whole thing. This is true of *Moby-Dick* and of the manual that came with your dishwasher. It falls out of the way word frequencies distribute themselves: a small handful of words doing enormous labor (*the*, *of*, *and*, tireless, invisible), and then a long tail of words that show up, do their one job, and are never called on again.

The technical term is *hapax legomenon* — "said once." Plural *hapax legomena*, which I like because it implies a category, a whole population of one-timers, a census of the unrepeated.

For a living language this is trivia. If a word appears once in a novel and you don't know it, you look it up, or you ask someone, or you wait and encounter it in a magazine three years later. The word exists elsewhere. But for a dead language, or a very old text, a hapax is a genuine crisis, because the only way anyone learns what a word means is triangulation. You see it in enough different rooms — enough contexts, enough sentences with enough surrounding scaffolding — that eventually the shape of the empty space in the middle becomes clear. A word said once gives you one room. Sometimes a very dark room.

The Hebrew Bible has hundreds of these. My favorite is in Genesis 6, where God tells Noah to build the ark out of *gopher* wood. Nobody knows what *gopher* wood is. The word occurs there and nowhere else in the entire corpus of ancient Hebrew, and there's no consensus etymology to fall back on. Cypress is the usual guess, mostly on the grounds that cypress is a sensible thing to build a boat out of and the consonants are vaguely suggestive. Some say cedar. Some think it might not be a species at all but a treatment — resinous wood, pitched wood, laminated wood. So the vessel that carries every living thing through the end of the world is made of a material we can't identify. Every translator who has ever handled that verse has had to put *something* there.

The Book of Job is thick with hapax legomena — it has more than almost anything else in the Bible, which is part of why Job is so hard, and why translations of it diverge so wildly. You can read two English versions side by side and find them describing different animals, different weather. The poetry is doing something extraordinary and we are partly guessing at what.

But here is the thing that keeps me coming back to this. In 1 Samuel 13, there's a passage about the Philistines controlling the ironworking trade, and it lists the prices Israelites had to pay to get their tools sharpened. One of the prices is a *pim*. The word appears nowhere else — not in the Bible, not in any other ancient Hebrew text. For centuries it was untranslatable. Translators fudged it, footnoted it, guessed. The King James Version doesn't even really try.

Then, in the early twentieth century, archaeologists digging in the Levant started turning up small stone weights, and some of them had a word scratched onto the side. *Pim.* They weigh about seven and a half grams — roughly two-thirds of a shekel. A unit of measure. The word had been sitting in the ground the whole time, in the hands of the people who had actually used it, waiting for someone to pick it up.

I find that story almost unbearably satisfying. The second occurrence wasn't in a text at all. It was in a stone.

There's an inverse to all this, which is even stranger: words that occur once and shouldn't occur at all. In 1934, the second edition of Webster's New International Dictionary included an entry for *dord*, a noun meaning density. It sat there for five years before an editor noticed it had no etymology and went looking. The trail led back to a slip of paper reading "D or d," submitted as an abbreviation for density, which someone had read as a single word and typeset accordingly. *Dord* had never been said by anyone. It was a hapax with no original utterance behind it — pure artifact, a word that existed only because a dictionary said so.

There are others. *Phantomnation* apparently entered the record because a line from Pope's *Odyssey* — "phantom nations of the dead" — passed through a reference work that printed compounds without spaces, and came out the other side as one word meaning "an appearance as of a phantom." Which is, you have to admit, an unusually apt accident. A ghost word meaning ghost.

I don't have a moral for this. But I notice that the same condition produces both cases: a thing said once cannot be checked against itself. It has to be interpreted rather than known, and interpretation is a bet. Most of the time the bet is invisible, absorbed into a translation choice or a dictionary entry, and everyone downstream inherits it as fact. Which is fine. That's most of how anything gets read.

Still. Somewhere out there the ark is being built, over and over, out of a wood no one can name.
